title: The Skyline Problem
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every building at every critical x-coordinate versus a sweep line over start/end events with a max-heap of active heights.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a list of buildings, each represented as [left, right, height], return the skyline formed by these buildings when viewed from a distance, as a list of "key points" [x, height] marking every location where the skyline's height changes, in left-to-right order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The skyline's height only changes where a building starts or ends","A sweep line over just those critical x-coordinates, not every possible x"],["At any point, the skyline's height is the tallest currently overlapping building","A max-heap of active building heights, updated as the sweep passes each building's start and end"]]}

blocks.text: Given a set of overlapping rectangular buildings, trace the outline of their combined silhouette, reporting only the x-coordinates where the outline's height actually changes.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracing a City Skyline From a Distance
blocks.text: Picture standing far from a city and tracing the outline formed by all its buildings together. The outline only changes shape where a building begins to block (or stops blocking) whatever was behind it, exactly the moments a building starts or ends.

blocks.caption: Sweeping left to right, the skyline height is always the tallest currently active building

blocks.text: Before checking every possible x-coordinate against every building, notice that the skyline's height only ever changes at a building's left or right edge, nowhere else.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Between any two consecutive building edges, no building starts or ends, so the tallest active building, and therefore the skyline height, cannot change.

Observation 2: This means only the x-coordinates where some building starts or ends need to be considered as candidate key points, not every integer x.

Observation 3: Sweeping through these edges left to right, while maintaining the set of "active" buildings (those whose range currently contains the sweep position), lets the current skyline height be read off as simply the maximum height among active buildings.

Observation 4: A max-heap of active building heights (with a mechanism to remove buildings once their right edge is passed) supports this efficiently, recording a new key point whenever the maximum height actually changes.
This leads to a sweep line over building start/end events, maintaining a max-heap of active heights, and emitting a key point whenever the maximum active height changes.

Collect every critical x-coordinate (every building's left and right edge). For each one, scan every building directly to find the tallest one covering that x, and record it if the height changed from the previous critical point.

items: Collect every building's left and right edge x-coordinates, sorted and de-duplicated.
For each critical x, scan every building, and note the maximum height of any building whose range includes x.
If that maximum differs from the previous critical point's height, record a new key point.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: at every critical x, scan all buildings directly for the tallest one covering it

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every candidate critical x is checked against every building directly, with no memory of which buildings were active at the previous critical point.
This correctly finds the tallest covering building each time, at the cost of a full re-scan for every candidate x.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), scanning every building for every one of up to 2n critical x-coordinates.
Space: O(n) for the critical x-coordinates and result.
Limitation: most buildings active at one critical point are still active at the next, but the brute force re-scans all of them every single time instead of tracking active buildings incrementally.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-scanning every building at every critical point is wasteful: a building only becomes active or inactive at its own start or end, it does not need to be re-checked at every OTHER building's edge too.

What structure tracks "currently active, tallest" efficiently: a max-heap of active building heights, where entering a building's range pushes its height, and passing its end removes it (lazily, by checking if a popped height's building has already ended).

How events are processed: sort all building start and end x-coordinates together; at a start event, push that building's height (with its end position, so it can be lazily removed later); at any event, discard heap entries whose building has already ended, and the new maximum height is the current skyline height.

The core idea: process events left to right in a single sweep, maintaining a max-heap of active heights, and record a new key point exactly when the maximum active height changes.

Create a start event and an end event for every building. Sort all events by x-coordinate (processing all events at the same x together, buildings starting before others end at that same x). Sweep through events, maintaining a max-heap of (height, end) pairs; before reading the current maximum, lazily discard any heap entries whose end has already passed. Whenever the maximum height changes, record a new key point.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one sweep over start/end events, max-heap tracks the tallest active building

blocks.text: Since the skyline can only change height at a building's start or end, processing exactly those events in order, while maintaining the tallest currently active building via a max-heap, captures every real change without re-examining buildings that are neither starting nor ending at the current event. Lazily discarding heap entries whose building has already ended keeps the heap's top always reflecting a truly active building.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), sorting 2n events, each heap operation O(log n).
Space: O(n) for the events and heap.

blocks.text: The Skyline Problem is a classic sweep-line application: process only the events where something actually changes (building starts or ends), and maintain the currently relevant maximum with a heap, rather than re-deriving it from scratch at every candidate point.

items: Not handling ties at the same x-coordinate correctly (a building starting exactly where another ends should be processed as starting first, so the skyline never dips to zero incorrectly).
Forgetting the sentinel ground-level (height 0) entry in the active set, which represents "no buildings currently active."
Not lazily removing ended buildings from the heap, letting stale, no-longer-active heights leak into the current maximum.

blocks.text: Explaining the event-sweep framing clearly, "the skyline only changes where a building starts or ends," and how a max-heap tracks the current tallest active building, demonstrates the key sweep-line insight before diving into heap mechanics.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every x-coordinate", think: only building start/end points are ever candidates for a skyline change.
If the interviewer says "how do you track the current tallest building efficiently", think: a max-heap of active heights, with lazy removal of buildings that have ended.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized sweep-line approach runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: sweep line over building start/end events, tracking the maximum active height with a heap.
Core Idea: the skyline only changes at a building's start or end; process those events in order, and record a new key point whenever the tallest currently active building changes.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized sweep-line approach.
Most Important Observation: only building edges are candidate skyline-change points; everything between two consecutive edges has a constant height.
Interview Difficulty: a classic hard problem; correctly handling event ordering ties and lazy heap removal are the trickiest details.
One line memory trick: sweep the edges, track the tallest active building with a heap, record every height change.
